papers.title_in_file: An Unsupervised Machine Learning to Optimize Hybrid Quantum Noise Clusters for Gaussian Quantum Channel
papers.partial_detail: Abstract, introduction (contributions), conclusion; system model, simulation sections and appendix skimmed only
papers.what_it_is: A simulation study that applies Gaussian mixture models and the EM algorithm to hybrid quantum noise in Gaussian quantum channels, aimed at satellite QKD.

assertions.value: The authors report that reducing the Gaussian clusters and applying the EM algorithm improves quantum channel capacity 11.8% without compromising essential hybrid noise components, validated through simulations.
assertions.anchor: Section I, contributions list, p.4; abstract
quotes: improves quantum channel capacity 11.8% without compromising essential hybrid noise components
The approach is validated through simulations
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical simulation result from one study.
assertions.reader_inference: The 11.8% figure is simulated channel capacity for a noise model, not a hardware result.

assertions.value: The authors report that their method reduces the number of Gaussian clusters with up to 15% error tolerance in Poisson weightage, ensuring accuracy 85%.
quotes: This method achieves up to 15% error tolerance in Poisson weightage, ensuring accuracy 85%
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical result from one study.

assertions.value: The authors state that the current study assumes a bi-variate hybrid quantum noise dataset, and that deep learning based clustering and hard clustering are left to future work.
quotes: The current study assumes a bi-variate hybrid quantum noise dataset, aligning with the system's specifications.
Future work will explore Deep Learning (DL)-based clustering methods and hard clustering approaches
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's own statement of its scope, Section I, p.4.

papers.title_in_file: Accelerating Parameter Initialization in Quantum Chemical Simulations via LSTM-FC-VQE
papers.partial_detail: Abstract, introduction, method overview, results text and Tables I and II discussion, conclusion; appendix skipped
papers.what_it_is: A simulation study of an LSTM meta-learner with a fully connected layer that predicts VQE initial parameters for molecules with different parameter counts.

assertions.value: The authors report that their fully connected LSTM model, trained with a constant learning rate and the Adam optimizer, reached an error of 0.048 mHa within only 86 iterations on the H4 molecule.
assertions.anchor: Section III, results discussion of Table I
quotes: our fully connected LSTM model, trained with a constant learning rate and the Adam optimizer, achieves a significantly lower error of 0.048 mHa within only 86 iterations
for the H4 molecule under four different parameter initialization strategies
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical simulation result from one study.

assertions.value: The authors report that on H4, random initialization followed by stochastic gradient descent needed 290 iterations to reach an error of 28.53 mHa, and LSTM initialization alone needed 357 iterations.
assertions.anchor: Section III, results discussion of Table I
quotes: random initialization followed by stochastic gradient descent (SGD) demands 290 iterations to reach an error of 28.53 mHa
Even with LSTM initialization alone, 357 iterations are needed
for the H4 molecule under four different parameter initialization strategies
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical simulation result from one study.
assertions.reader_inference: The 357 versus 290 iterations shows the base LSTM alone was slower than random initialization in this run.

assertions.value: The authors report that on H2O their fully connected LSTM VQE model reached a comparable VQE-quality baseline in just 78 iterations, and they cite a prior VQE study that required over 2500 iterations to reach that energy level.
assertions.anchor: Section III, results discussion of Table II
quotes: For more complex systems such as H2O, the standard VQE typically converges
required over 2500 iterations to reach this energy level
our fully connected LSTMVQE model achieves a comparable VQE-quality baseline in just 78 iterations
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical result from one study, compared against a cited result.
assertions.reader_inference: The comparison is against a different study's setup, not a matched run.

assertions.value: The authors state that for complex molecules, further improvement in absolute accuracy may require enhancements to the underlying VQE framework itself, and report a final predicted energy within 50 mHa of the FCI reference value.
assertions.anchor: Section III, results discussion of Fig. 4 and Table II
quotes: achieving further improvements in absolute accuracy for complex molecules may require enhancements to the underlying VQE framework itself
the final predicted energy achieves an error within 50 mHa of the FCI reference value
assertions.certainty_reason: Mixed empirical result and author remark; the 50 mHa figure is from one run.
assertions.reader_inference: 50 mHa is far above chemical accuracy (about 1.6 mHa), so the H2O result is not chemically accurate.

papers.title_in_file: Solving various NP-Hard problems using exponentially fewer qubits on a Quantum Computer
papers.partial_detail: Abstract, introduction, circuit-depth discussion, scalability results text, run-time discussion, conclusion start; encoding derivations and tables skimmed
papers.what_it_is: A paper extending a logarithmic-qubit encoding of Maximum Cut to other NP-hard problems and testing it on a simulator and a real quantum computer.

assertions.value: The paper states that a Maximum Cut problem with a graph of n nodes can be represented using only ⌈log2 n⌉ qubits, building on an earlier algorithm.
quotes: a Maximum Cut problem with a graph of n nodes can be represented using only ⌈log2 n⌉ qubits
assertions.certainty_reason: The encoding is attributed to earlier work [26].

assertions.value: The authors state that their circuit uses |V | − 1 CNOT gates, where |V | is the number of vertices, against p|E| for the QAOA ansatz, and conclude the circuit is much shallower.
quotes: The number of CNOT gates required for the QAOA ansatz is p|E|
In our algorithm the number of CNOTs is equal to |V | − 1, |V | being the number of vertices.
assertions.certainty_reason: Gate count argued by the authors; the QAOA count rests on a cited assumption about depth.

assertions.value: The authors report that on Maximum Cut instances up to graph sizes of 256, run on a simulator and a real quantum computer, the results are nearly or over 90% of the optimal cut found by an ILP solver.
quotes: these algorithms are tested on a quantum simulator with graph sizes of over a hundred nodes and on a real quantum computer up to graph sizes of 256
We can see that for all cases, the results are nearly or over 90% of the optimal cut.
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical result from one study.
assertions.reader_inference: The 90% statement is in the paragraph on the 64, 128 and 256 node simulator runs; the exact scope of 'all cases' is a table the reader did not check.

assertions.value: The authors state that the real-world time on the quantum computer was several hours or even several days for the largest run instance, which prevented larger instances.
quotes: The real-world time was several hours or even several days for the largest run instance.
This prevented us from running larger instances on the quantum computer.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's own statement of why hardware runs stopped at its largest size, Section III.

papers.title_in_file: Towards a scalable discrete quantum generative adversarial neural network
papers.partial_detail: Abstract, introduction, Ising results, methods, discussion and outlook; B&S dataset and appendices skimmed
papers.what_it_is: A simulated fully quantum GAN for binary data, tested on a synthetic dataset and on low energy states of an Ising model.

assertions.value: The authors report that the average energy of the training states is −3.0 and of the generator's states −2.6, and after removing the training states from the samples the average energy is still negative, at −0.34.
assertions.anchor: Section IV, Ising results, Fig. 8, p.7
quotes: While the average energy of the training states is −3.0, the states produced by the generator have an average energy of −2.6
we remove the training states from the samples generated by G and the average energy is still negative, at −0.34
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical simulation result from one study.

assertions.value: The authors describe the Ising test as a proof-of-concept and state that tests on larger systems and more complicated Hamiltonians are left for future work.
quotes: This test serves as a proof-of-concept of using the QGAN to generalize from low energy Ising states.
We leave these tests for future work.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's own statement of scope, Section IV, p.8.

assertions.value: The authors state that for the hardware efficient ansatz barren plateaus will make training for a large number of qubits impossible, and that it is not clear how the required circuit depth scales with input size and qubit count.
quotes: for the given hardware efficient circuit ansatz, barren plateaus will make the training for a large number of qubits impossible
it is not clear yet how the required depth of the quantum circuit scales with the size of the input data and the number of qubits
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's own stated limit on scalability, Section VI.

assertions.value: The authors state that the QGAN tends to converge to a distribution with zero probabilities for certain states, even states in the training dataset, and that the precise cause requires further investigation.
quotes: the QGAN tends to converge to a distribution that has zero probabilities for certain states
the precise cause of the phenomenon requires further investigation
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's own stated limitation, Section IV, p.8.

papers.title_in_file: Foundations of Quantum Federated Learning Over Classical and Quantum Networks
papers.partial_detail: Abstract, introduction, classical-network challenges, conclusion and recommendations start; quantum-network section skimmed
papers.what_it_is: A perspective paper that surveys challenges and proposed directions for quantum federated learning over classical and quantum networks, with no experiments in the sections read.

assertions.value: The authors state that this paper is the first comprehensive investigation of the challenges and opportunities of quantum federated learning.
quotes: In this paper, we provide the first comprehensive investigation of the challenges and opportunities of QFL.
assertions.certainty_reason: Priority claim by the authors.

assertions.value: The authors state that local gate noise in NISQ devices is embedded in the learning parameters of QFL clients, making useful information hard to separate from noise at the server.
quotes: This intrinsic local noise, produced during the training phase, will be inextricably integrated into the learning parameters, i.e., the quantum circuit parameters.
assertions.certainty_reason: Argued challenge without an experiment in this paper.

assertions.value: The authors state, citing earlier work, that as the number of clients with non-uniform and non-IID data increases, the necessary number of global communication rounds escalates.
quotes: As the number of clients with non-uniform and non-IID data participating in QFL increases, the necessary number of global communication rounds to accomplish training escalates accordingly [5].
assertions.certainty_reason: Attributed to cited work [5].

assertions.value: The authors recommend measuring quantum advantage, stating that identifying when QFL outperforms classical FL requires advanced algorithms and benchmarks for accurate comparisons.
quotes: Identifying when QFL outperforms classical FL requires advanced algorithms and benchmarks for accurate comparisons.
assertions.certainty_reason: Author recommendation; no comparison is run in the sections read.
assertions.reader_inference: The paper treats the QFL advantage over classical FL as not yet established.

papers.partial_detail: Abstract, introduction, numerical results text, measurement-count discussion, conclusions; appendices skimmed
papers.what_it_is: A simulation study that trains shallow quantum circuits with Adam to discriminate non-orthogonal quantum states and compares them with optimal POVMs.

assertions.value: The authors report that numerical simulations show shallow quantum circuits could be trained to discriminate among various pure and mixed quantum states with comparable performance to theoretically optimal POVMs.
quotes: shallow quantum circuits could be trained to discriminate among various pure and mixed quantum states
comparable performance to theoretically optimal POVMs
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical simulation result from one study.

assertions.value: The authors report that, with a high penalty forcing the error probability near zero, training did not on average reach the theoretical minimum inconclusiveness, and that a small non-zero error allowed a much lower inconclusiveness.
quotes: we did not reach on average the theoretical minimum inconclusiveness Pinc when we use a high penalty to force the error probability Perr to be close to zero
we are able to obtain much smaller Pinc by accepting small non-zero Perr
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical simulation result from one study.

assertions.value: The authors state that the experiment was done on a simulated quantum computer, on classical hardware where exact measurement probabilities are available, and report that a repeated-measurement cost function was within 3% error of the exact value with a relative standard deviation of 13%.
quotes: Although this experiment was done on a simulated quantum computers, i.e., classical hardware, where exact measurement probabilities are available
the final cost function is close to the value obtained with the exact probability (with an error within 3%) and is stable (with a relative standard deviation of 13%)
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's own statement that results come from simulation, Section 5.

papers.title_in_file: Variational Quantum Circuits for Deep Reinforcement Learning
papers.partial_detail: Abstract, introduction, performance analysis, hardware test text, discussions, conclusions; appendices skipped
papers.what_it_is: A paper that builds variational quantum circuit deep Q-learning agents and tests them in frozen-lake and cognitive-radio environments, in simulation and on a 5-qubit IBM machine.

assertions.value: The authors report that in the cognitive-radio experiment with 2, 3, 4 and 5 possible channels they ran 500 episodes and the agent converges to the optimal total reward at around 100 iterations or episodes.
quotes: In the cognitive-radio experiment, we tested situations where there are 2, 3, 4 and 5 possible channels
we run 500 episodes and the agent converges to the optimal total reward value at around 100 iterations or episodes
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical simulation result from one study.

assertions.value: The authors report that in a simulation with the noise model from an IBM quantum machine, the agent converges to the optimal total reward at around 110 iterations in the 2-channel and 4-channel settings, and they conclude the approach is robust against noise in current machines.
quotes: the agent converges to the optimal total reward value at around 110 iterations in the 2-channel and 4-channel settings
showing that our proposed quantum circuit based DRL is robust against noise in the current machines
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical simulation result from one study.
assertions.reader_inference: Robustness is shown on small environments with a device noise model, not on a large task.

assertions.value: The authors state that for the considered testing environments variational quantum deep Q-learning involves parameters as small as O(n), against O(n3) for tabular Q-learning and O(n2) for neural network based deep Q-learning, and describe this as quantum advantage in memory and parameter count.
quotes: the variational quantum deep Q-learning involves parameters as small as O(n), but the tabular Q-learning and neural network based deep Q-learning have O(n3) and O(n2) parameters, respectively.
assertions.certainty_reason: Author claim about parameter scaling in the tested environments.
assertions.reader_inference: This is a parameter-count advantage, not a speed advantage, and rests on the computational-basis encoding used here.

assertions.value: The authors state that they use simple testing environments to study feasibility, and that the number of qubits needed for mainstream benchmark environments is intractable for classical simulation and exceeds currently available quantum devices.
assertions.anchor: Section VII-B, more complex testing environments
quotes: we use simple testing environments to study the feasibility of quantum circuits-based DQL (DQN)
the number of qubits needed is intractable for numerical simulations on classical computers and also exceeds currently commercially available quantum devices
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's own statement of its scope, Section VII-B.

papers.title_in_file: Asynchronous training of quantum reinforcement learning
papers.partial_detail: Abstract, introduction, hyperparameters and model size, results for Acrobot, CartPole and MiniGrid, conclusion; background sections skimmed
papers.what_it_is: A numerical-simulation study of asynchronous advantage actor-critic training for variational quantum policies against classical agents of similar size.

assertions.value: The authors report that in the Cart-Pole environment over 100,000 episodes the quantum model achieved significantly higher scores than the classical model, although the classical model learned faster early in training.
assertions.anchor: Section VI, Cart-Pole results, Fig. 8, p.13
quotes: The next experiment was conducted in the Cart-Pole environment. The total number of episodes was 100,000.
the quantum model achieved significantly higher scores than the classical model
While the classical model demonstrated faster learning in the early training episodes, the quantum model eventually surpassed it
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical simulation result from one study.

assertions.value: The authors report that in the MiniGrid-SimpleCrossing environment the quantum model outperformed the classical model in two of the three scenarios.
assertions.anchor: Section VI, MiniGrid results, Fig. 9, p.13
quotes: the quantum model outperformed the classical model in two of the three scenarios
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical simulation result from one study.
assertions.reader_inference: Two of three scenarios, read off simulated learning curves, is weak evidence of a general quantum edge.

assertions.value: The authors state that results are from numerical simulations of an 8 qubit VQC with two variational layers, 96 quantum parameters in total, and 80 parallel agents, compared with classical agents of similar model size, within the tasks considered.
assertions.anchor: Abstract; Section VI-B hyperparameters and model size
quotes: We demonstrate the results via numerical simulations that within the tasks considered
For the VQC, we set the number of qubits to be 8 and two variational layers are used.
the total number of quantum parameters is 96
The number of CPU cores and hence the number of parallel agents is 80 in this work.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's own statement of its setup and scope, Section VI-B.
assertions.reader_inference: All results are classical simulation of the circuits; no quantum hardware run is reported in the sections read.
